context.transcript:
Dialogue 1.
W: Good morning, Silk Road Hotel. How can I help you?
M: Hello, I'd like to book a room for the fifth of May, please. A double room.
W: Certainly, sir. One double room for the fifth of May.
M: Actually, sorry — my colleague is travelling with me, so we'd better have a twin room, with two separate beds.
W: No problem at all. A twin room for the fifth of May. That's sixty dollars a night, breakfast included.

Dialogue 2.
M: Good afternoon, City Clinic. How can I help?
W: Hello, I'd like to see Dr Alimova, please. Is she free on Tuesday afternoon?
M: Let me check... Yes, she has a free appointment at three o'clock on Tuesday.
W: Oh dear, I work until five on Tuesdays. Is there anything on Wednesday morning?
M: There's a free slot at ten o'clock on Wednesday.
W: Perfect, I'll take that one. Thank you.

Dialogue 3.
M: You look worried. What's wrong?
W: I can't find my phone anywhere! I think I left it in the taxi this morning.
M: Did you call the taxi company?
W: I was about to, but wait... actually, I remember using it at the café when I paid for my coffee. I must have left it on the table there.
M: Then let's ring the café right now — someone has probably handed it in.

Dialogue 4.
M: Hi, how much is a monthly membership at this gym?
W: It's normally three hundred thousand som a month, and that includes the swimming pool.
M: Hmm, that's a bit expensive for me. I'm a university student.
W: Oh, in that case you get our student discount — you'd only pay two hundred thousand som a month.
M: Great, I'll sign up today then.

Dialogue 5.
W: Excuse me, is the two o'clock train to Bukhara on time?
M: I'm afraid not, madam. There was a problem on the line, so at first they announced a delay of twenty minutes.
W: Twenty minutes? That's not too bad.
M: Well, actually, they've just announced that it will now leave forty minutes late, at twenty to three.
W: Forty minutes! I'd better go and get some tea, then.

Dialogue 6.
M: It's Nilufar's birthday on Friday. What should we get her?
W: How about a nice scarf? She loves fashion.
M: She got three scarves last year. What about a book?
W: Hmm, she mostly listens to audiobooks these days. Actually, you know her old headphones are broken — let's buy her a good pair of headphones.
M: Perfect idea. She'll use them every single day.

Dialogue 7.
W: Are we still having the picnic on Saturday?
M: I've just checked the forecast — heavy rain all day on Saturday, I'm afraid.
W: Oh no. What about Sunday?
M: Sunday looks sunny and warm, about twenty-five degrees.
W: Then let's move the picnic to Sunday and go to the cinema on Saturday instead.
M: Sounds like a plan.

Dialogue 8.
W: Are you ready to order, sir?
M: Yes, I'd like the lagman, please.
W: I'm very sorry, but the lagman is finished for today. The plov is excellent, though — it's just been made.
M: All right, I'll have the plov then, and a fresh salad on the side.
W: Certainly. And to drink?
M: Just green tea, please.

M: Hi Malika, you look deep in thought. What's up?
W: Hi Timur. I have to submit my university application by Friday, and I still can't decide between economics and computer science.
M: Really? I thought you'd already chosen economics. Your father is an economist, isn't he?
W: He is, and at first I simply wanted to follow in his footsteps. But last month I took part in a two-week programming camp, and honestly, I loved every minute of it. That's when I realised computer science suits me much better.
M: Fair enough. What about the job market, though?
W: That's actually another reason. The IT park in our city works with foreign companies, and they hire hundreds of graduates every year. Several of my friends who finished economics spent almost a year looking for their first job.
M: That's a strong argument. Have you talked to anyone at the university about the course itself?
W: Not yet. I was planning to email the admissions office this week.
M: Emails take ages, and the answers are always so general. You know, the university is holding an open day this Friday. Why don't we go together? You can meet the computer science professors, and I want to have a look at the engineering department anyway.
W: That's a brilliant idea. Let's meet at the main gate at ten o'clock.
M: Deal. And bring your questions written down, so you don't forget anything.
W: Good thinking. Thanks, Timur — I feel much better about this now.

context.transcript:
W: Good evening, listeners, and welcome back to Business Voices. Today in our studio we have Jasur Rakhimov, who at just twenty-four runs one of the most popular coffee shops in Tashkent. Jasur, welcome to the programme.
M: Thank you for inviting me. It's a pleasure to be here.
W: Let's start at the beginning. Where did the idea for your coffee shop come from?
M: Well, during my third year at university I spent two semesters in Seoul, in South Korea, as an exchange student, and I worked part-time as a barista there. I noticed that coffee shops in Korea were not just places to drink coffee — people studied there, worked there, met their friends there. I fell in love with that culture and I wanted to bring it home to Tashkent.
W: Many people believe the hardest part of starting a business is finding the money. Was that true for you?
M: Surprisingly, no. I received a young entrepreneurs' loan from the bank quite quickly — the paperwork took only three weeks. The real difficulty was finding the right location. I must have looked at more than thirty places over four months before I finally found a corner building near the university.
W: And how did you attract your very first customers?
M: We had almost no money left for advertising, so I simply started posting short videos on social media, showing exactly how we roast our beans and make our drinks. One of those videos got over a million views, and the next morning there was a queue outside the door before we even opened.
W: That's incredible. I've also heard your café is a little unusual. Tell us about that.
M: Yes — every Wednesday evening we hold a free English speaking club. Students practise with volunteers, and of course they usually buy a coffee or two while they're there. It brings the community together, and honestly, it has turned out to be the best advertising we've ever had.
W: So what's next for Jasur Rakhimov?
M: Next spring we're opening our second branch — not in Tashkent, but in Samarkand. My dream is to have a café in every big city of Uzbekistan one day.
W: We wish you luck. That was Jasur Rakhimov, everyone.

parts.titleEn: Part 6: Lecture — the history of the Silk Road (Questions 30-35)
parts.instructionsEn: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of the Silk Road. For each question, choose the correct answer (A-D).
parts.instructionsUz: Buyuk Ipak yo'li tarixi haqidagi ma'ruzaning bir qismini eshitasiz. Har bir savol uchun to'g'ri javobni tanlang.

context.transcript:
Good afternoon, everyone. In today's lecture we're going to look at the history of the Silk Road — perhaps the most famous trade network in human history.

First of all, despite its name, the Silk Road was not a single road at all. It was a vast network of routes, stretching for more than six thousand kilometres, which connected China with the Mediterranean world for roughly one and a half thousand years. Merchants rarely travelled the whole distance; instead, goods changed hands many times along the way.

Interestingly, the name itself is surprisingly modern. It was invented not by the traders who used the routes, but by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, in the nineteenth century — hundreds of years after the routes had lost their importance.

Silk, of course, was the most famous product carried west from China. But merchants also traded paper, spices, glass, silver and horses. Paper is a particularly good example: the secret of paper-making travelled from China through Samarkand, and from there it eventually reached Europe, changing the history of knowledge forever.

However — and this is the key point of today's lecture — the Silk Road carried far more than goods. Religions such as Buddhism and Islam, together with scientific ideas, artistic styles, music and even new foods, spread along exactly the same routes. In that sense, you could call the Silk Road the internet of the ancient world: it connected distant cultures and let ideas travel as fast as camels could walk.

Cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara grew enormously rich because of their position on these routes. Caravans of camels needed food, water, fresh animals and safe places to rest, and these cities provided everything a tired merchant could possibly want. Their bazaars became legendary across three continents.

So why did it all come to an end? From the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries onwards, European ships began sailing directly to India and China. Transporting goods by sea was simply cheaper and safer than the long journey across mountains and deserts, and slowly the great overland routes lost their traffic, and the caravan cities lost their wealth.

Next week, we'll look at how modern railway projects are trying to revive these ancient connections. Thank you.

parts.passageText:
How Sport Changes the Brain

A. Scientists have discovered that regular physical activity has a direct effect on the hippocampus, the part of the brain responsible for storing new information. In one famous experiment, adults who walked briskly three times a week for a year actually increased the size of this brain region, while a non-exercising control group saw it shrink. The walkers also performed noticeably better on tests in which they had to recall lists of words and faces.

B. When we feel pressure at work or before an exam, our bodies release the hormone cortisol, which in large amounts can damage brain cells. Exercise offers a powerful defence. Even twenty minutes of jogging, swimming or dancing causes the brain to release endorphins — natural chemicals that lower cortisol levels and create a feeling of calm that can last for hours after the activity ends.

C. Teachers have long noticed that pupils behave better after PE lessons, and neuroscience now explains why. Short periods of movement increase blood flow to the prefrontal cortex, the brain area that controls attention. In schools where children do twenty minutes of morning exercise, pupils stay concentrated on tasks for longer and are less easily distracted during lessons.

D. For most of the twentieth century, scientists believed that adults could never grow new brain cells — the brain you had at twenty was the brain you would die with. We now know this is wrong. Physical activity stimulates the birth of new neurons, a process called neurogenesis, and remarkably, this has been observed even in people in their seventies and eighties.

E. The benefits of sport continue after the sun goes down. People who exercise regularly fall asleep faster, wake up less often during the night, and spend more time in deep sleep — the stage in which the brain washes away the waste products that build up during the day. This nightly cleaning process is believed to protect the brain against diseases of old age.

F. Not all of sport's effects on the brain come from movement itself. Team games such as football, basketball and volleyball force players to read their teammates' intentions, predict opponents' actions and communicate under pressure. Psychologists say this constant social calculation is a workout for the brain's social circuits, and young team players tend to develop stronger cooperation skills than those who train alone.

parts.passageText:
The Story of Chocolate

Today chocolate is one of the most popular foods on Earth, but its story began more than three thousand years ago in the rainforests of Central America. The peoples of the region — first the Olmecs, later the Maya and the Aztecs — were the first to discover the secret of the cacao tree. They did not eat chocolate, however; they drank it. Cacao beans were roasted, ground into a paste and mixed with water, chilli pepper and spices to make a cold, bitter drink called "xocolatl", which was served at religious ceremonies and royal feasts.

For the Aztecs, cacao was far more than a food. The beans were so valuable that they were used as money: historical records show that a rabbit cost about ten beans, while a turkey cost two hundred. Emperor Montezuma was said to drink fifty cups of chocolate a day, believing it gave him strength and wisdom.

Everything changed in the sixteenth century, when Spanish explorers brought cacao beans back to Europe. The bitter drink did not please European tastes at first, so the Spanish made one small change with enormous consequences: they replaced the chilli with sugar. Sweet drinking chocolate quickly became the favourite luxury of the Spanish court, and within a hundred years fashionable chocolate houses had opened in Madrid, Paris and London. Even then, chocolate remained something people drank, not ate.

The chocolate bar as we know it is a surprisingly recent invention. It was not until 1847 that the British company Fry's discovered how to mix cocoa powder, cocoa butter and sugar into a solid bar that could be moulded and sold in shops. Twenty-eight years later, in 1875, the Swiss inventor Daniel Peter, after eight years of failed experiments, finally succeeded in adding milk to the recipe, with help from his neighbour Henri Nestlé, who produced condensed milk. Milk chocolate was born, and Switzerland's reputation as the home of fine chocolate was established.

Today the geography of chocolate is truly global — and rather surprising. Although chocolate is mostly eaten in Europe and North America, almost none of the raw material grows there. About sixty per cent of the world's cacao is now produced by just two West African countries, Ivory Coast and Ghana, thousands of kilometres from the plant's original home. Meanwhile, the world championship in eating chocolate belongs firmly to the Swiss, who consume around ten kilograms per person every year — roughly two hundred bars each.

parts.passageText:
Learning to Code as a Second Career

More and more adults in their thirties and forties are leaving stable jobs to learn computer programming. [15] Dilnoza Karimova, a 34-year-old former accountant from Tashkent, is one of them.

She first became interested in coding when her company introduced new accounting software. [16] Instead of feeling annoyed like everyone else, Dilnoza became curious — she wanted to understand how the program actually worked on the inside.

At first, she studied alone in the evenings, using free online courses. [17] So she joined a local coding bootcamp, where she could ask teachers questions face to face and practise on real projects with other students.

The change was far from easy. [18] For six months she had no income at all, and there were moments when she seriously considered giving up and returning to her old profession.

Her first job applications were all rejected. [19] Finally, a small IT company offered her a junior position — partly, they admitted later, because her accounting background was exactly what they needed for the financial software they were building.

Today, two years later, Dilnoza earns more than she ever did as an accountant. [20] She believes her story proves that it is never too late to change direction.

[21] Recruitment specialists say that the combination of life experience, discipline and fresh technical skills makes career changers surprisingly valuable to employers — often more valuable than young graduates.

parts.passageText:
Should Homework Be Abolished?

Few school topics cause as much argument at the dinner table as homework. In recent years, several school systems — from parts of the United States to whole regions of Spain — have experimented with reducing it or banning it altogether, and every such announcement is greeted with cheers from children and heated debate among adults.

Those who want to abolish homework make three main points. First, they argue that after a six- or seven-hour school day, children need rest, play and family time; instead, many spend their evenings hunched over worksheets, and doctors report rising levels of stress and poor sleep among pupils as young as ten. Second, homework quietly deepens inequality. A child with a quiet room, a laptop and university-educated parents completes the same task in half the time it takes a classmate who shares a small flat with noisy siblings and has nobody to ask for help. The task is identical; the conditions are not. Third, the research is surprisingly weak: studies repeatedly show that homework in primary school makes almost no measurable difference to academic results.

Supporters of this view often point to Finland, where school days are short, homework is minimal, and yet students regularly perform near the top of international rankings. The example is attractive, but it should be treated with caution: Finland also has exceptionally well-trained teachers, small classes and a strong reading culture, so it is impossible to say how much of its success — if any — is explained by the lack of homework.

Defenders of homework, meanwhile, have evidence of their own. In secondary school, moderate amounts of homework — around an hour a day — are consistently linked with better exam results. More importantly, they argue, homework teaches something no classroom can: the ability to organise your own time, struggle with a problem alone, and finish a task without a teacher standing over you. These are precisely the skills that university students and employees need most, and pupils who never practise them at school often struggle badly later.

My own view is that both camps are attacking the wrong target. The real problem is not homework itself but its quality. There is a world of difference between a photocopied worksheet of twenty identical exercises and a task that asks a child to interview a grandparent, design an experiment or read a chapter of a real book. Schools should set less homework, and better homework — meaningful tasks that children can complete independently, whatever their home conditions. Banning homework entirely, however tempting the headline, would be throwing the baby out with the bathwater.

parts.passageText:
Water Scarcity in Central Asia

Central Asia is a region defined by water. Its two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, rise in the high mountains of Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan and flow for thousands of kilometres through deserts and steppes, supporting the lives of more than seventy million people. Yet today the region faces one of the most serious water crises on Earth — a crisis that is largely of human making.

The story begins in the 1960s, when Soviet planners decided to turn the deserts of Central Asia into enormous fields of cotton, a crop so profitable it was known as "white gold". Gigantic canals were dug to carry river water to the new plantations. The plan succeeded — the region became one of the world's leading cotton producers — but the price was catastrophic. So much water was taken from the two rivers that the Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake in the world, began to disappear. By the early twenty-first century it had lost around ninety per cent of its volume, and fishing ports that once employed thousands of people found themselves sixty kilometres from the water's edge.

The consequences reach far beyond the vanished fishing industry. The exposed seabed, covered with salt and agricultural chemicals, has become the source of violent dust storms that carry toxic particles hundreds of kilometres, and doctors in the region report unusually high rates of respiratory disease. The loss of the sea's moderating influence has even changed the local climate, making summers hotter and winters colder.

Agriculture remains at the heart of the problem. It consumes roughly ninety per cent of all water used in the region, and much of that water never reaches a single plant: it evaporates from open canals or leaks into the sand through unlined channels built half a century ago. Engineers estimate that simply repairing and covering the main canals could save enough water to supply millions of people. Modern techniques offer further hope. Drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of each plant through narrow pipes, can cut water use by up to half while actually increasing harvests; yet it is still used on only a small fraction of the region's farmland, mainly because of the initial cost.

The future adds a further complication. The glaciers of Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, which act as frozen reservoirs feeding the rivers through the hot summer months, are melting at an alarming rate as the climate warms. Scientists warn that river flows could fall significantly by the middle of the century, just as the region's growing population needs more water than ever.

No single country can solve this crisis alone, for the rivers ignore national borders: water saved upstream is water gained downstream. The states of Central Asia have begun to cooperate more closely in recent years, sharing data and coordinating the use of reservoirs. Such cooperation, most experts agree, is not merely desirable — it is the region's only realistic path to water security.
